analysis.one_liner: Cuts and caps US nuclear weapons programs, including the new land-based missile, low-yield warheads, and space-based missile defenses.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote; the nuclear weapons programs it targeted — which the CBO estimated would cost about $634 billion between fiscal years 2021 and 2030 — continued as planned.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, known as the SANE Act, would have shrunk the US nuclear arsenal and canceled or capped roughly a dozen nuclear weapons programs. It would have capped the force at 1,000 deployed strategic warheads, limited the new Columbia-class submarine fleet to eight boats, blocked the Air Force's next-generation land-based missile, banned low-yield nuclear warheads, prohibited space-based missile defenses, and killed the new nuclear cruise missile and its warhead. It would also have required the Pentagon and the Department of Energy to report to Congress on the cost savings and given the public an annual accounting of what each nuclear weapon actually costs. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers would benefit from the savings: the bill cites CBO estimates of roughly $634 billion in planned nuclear spending over the 2021–2030 decade and $1.7 trillion through 2046, with tens of billions in achievable savings even while keeping a full nuclear triad. Ordinary people would also gain from oversight provisions requiring an annual public accounting of what each nuclear weapon costs over its life cycle, and communities like Oak Ridge, Tennessee and Los Alamos, New Mexico would be spared the environmental and fiscal risks of expanded plutonium and uranium processing. Money freed from nuclear programs could go toward the conventional forces the Pentagon's own leadership said it could not afford to modernize at the same time.

how_it_helps.text: It would cap the nuclear force at roughly one-third below New START levels: no more than eight Columbia-class submarines, 150 land-based ICBMs, 80 B-21 bombers, and 1,000 deployed strategic warheads.

It would kill or cap roughly a dozen specific weapons programs, including the new ground-based ICBM, the new long-range air-launched cruise missile and its W80 warhead, low-yield nuclear warheads like the W76-2, space-based missile defense, and the W93 submarine warhead.

It would require the Defense and Energy Departments to report annually on the cost savings produced by the cuts and require the President to send Congress a yearly accounting of what every nuclear weapon and program actually costs over its lifetime.

analysis.who_pays: Nuclear weapons contractors and the Department of Energy's weapons complex would lose contracts worth hundreds of billions: the new ICBM, the new nuclear cruise missile, new warhead production, the Oak Ridge uranium processing plant, and expanded plutonium pit production. Workers and local economies in Tennessee and New Mexico tied to those facilities would bear job losses. Defense officials who believe the full modernization is necessary for deterrence against Russia and China would lose the programs they sought.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nuclear weapons contractors and their workers

drawbacks.text: Supporters of full nuclear modernization argue the current arsenal is aging and must be replaced to maintain a credible deterrent against Russia and China; the bill would cancel the new land-based ICBM entirely and cap deployed warheads at 1,000, changes opponents say would weaken deterrence and could be read by rivals as American retrenchment.

The bill would concentrate losses in specific communities: it terminates the Uranium Processing Facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee and caps plutonium pit production at Los Alamos, New Mexico, so the jobs and local economies tied to the nuclear weapons complex would bear the cost of the savings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest case for the bill was fiscal: the CBO estimated tens of billions in savings over a decade just from trimming current plans, and the bill's own findings cite GAO warnings that the nuclear complex could not afford all its simultaneous billion-dollar projects. The strongest objection is deterrence: supporters of the full modernization program argue that an aging triad must be replaced to remain credible against Russia and China, and that canceling the new ICBM and low-yield options would narrow the President's choices rather than responsibly right-size the arsenal. The bill as written was maximalist — it did not just trim, it barred roughly a dozen named programs outright — so a fair reading is that the goal was defensible and the specific list was open to debate. None of that debate happened: the bill received no hearing or vote, so neither the savings nor any deterrent risk was ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Armed Services Committee, where the bill sat after its referral, never took it up, and the two-year Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no action of any kind after introduction.

narrative.text: The complete action history consists of two entries: introduction on May 26, 2021 and a referral to the Committee on Armed Services the same day.

The bill would have barred spending on the new ground-based ICBM, the long-range stand-off cruise missile and its W80 warhead, low-yield warheads like the W76-2, space-based missile defense, and the Uranium Processing Facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.

The bill cited a January 2019 CBO estimate that the US would spend about $634 billion between fiscal years 2021 and 2030 to maintain and rebuild its nuclear force, and a December 2020 CBO analysis showing $12.4 to $13.6 billion in savings from trimming current plans while keeping all three legs of the nuclear triad.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors and the nuclear weapons establishment came out ahead: every program the bill targeted, from the new ICBM to the low-yield warheads, continued with its funding stream intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nuclear weapons contractors and the Pentagon

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: Senate Armed Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the roughly nineteen months it had jurisdiction, from referral in May 2021 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Jack Reed
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during his chairmanship of the panel to which it was referred.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never measured; the bill's only backers were one Democrat and one Independent, and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Nuclear weapons contractors and the DOE weapons complex
industries.note: The bill would cancel or cap programs these contractors were counting on for decades of revenue: the new ICBM, the new cruise missile and its warhead, new warhead production, the Oak Ridge uranium facility, and expanded plutonium pit work. Because the bill died without a vote, these contracts continued untouched.

industries.industry: Military shipbuilders, aircraft makers, and missile manufacturers
industries.note: The bill still allows eight Columbia-class submarines and 80 B-21 bombers, so it narrows rather than ends work at yards like Electric Boat and plants like Northrop's bomber line. It cancels the next-generation ICBM outright and bars an F-35 nuclear role.

The bill's findings argue that nuclear modernization is crowding out the conventional forces the Pentagon says it needs to compete with Russia and China, so the freed money could flow to ships, planes, and troops instead of warheads.
